lessonTitle: Cholinergic and Anticholinergic Drugs: Muscarinic and Nicotinic Pharmacology

blocks.text: A 30-year-old woman notices her eyelids droop and her words slur by the end of the day, but both recover after rest. A drug that prevents the breakdown of one neurotransmitter restores her strength within minutes. Understanding why requires knowing exactly how acetylcholine works at the neuromuscular junction, and what happens when its actions are enhanced or blocked.

blocks.markdown: **Acetylcholine (ACh)** is the transmitter of all preganglionic autonomic neurons, postganglionic parasympathetic neurons, somatic motor neurons and some sympathetic postganglionic neurons (sweat glands). It acts on two receptor families: **nicotinic** receptors (ligand-gated ion channels at ganglia and the neuromuscular junction) and **muscarinic** receptors (M1 to M5, G-protein-coupled; at parasympathetic target organs and sweat glands). ACh is broken down within milliseconds by **acetylcholinesterase (AChE)** in the synaptic cleft.

blocks.title: Antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) drug
blocks.text: An antimuscarinic drug competitively blocks muscarinic receptors, preventing ACh from acting on parasympathetic target organs. Atropine is the prototype. The term anticholinergic is often used in the same sense, though it strictly includes nicotinic blockers too.

blocks.caption: Effects of muscarinic blockade by atropine, by organ.
rows: Tachycardia; used to treat symptomatic bradycardia
Dry mouth, dry skin and reduced sweating
Used as inhaled antimuscarinic bronchodilators (for example ipratropium); reduces secretions pre-operatively

blocks.title: Predicting the effects of an antimuscarinic
blocks.prompt: A patient takes a drug with strong antimuscarinic action. Predict four symptoms and explain each in terms of blocked parasympathetic function.

steps.text: Start from the principle: the parasympathetic system promotes rest-and-digest. Blocking muscarinic receptors removes that tone.
Salivary glands lose secretory drive, so the mouth is dry. Sweat glands (sympathetic cholinergic, muscarinic) also stop secreting, so the skin is dry and the patient may overheat.
The bladder detrusor cannot contract, producing hesitancy or retention; the gut slows, producing constipation.
The iris sphincter is unopposed by parasympathetic constriction, causing a dilated pupil, and the SA node loses vagal restraint, giving a faster heart rate.

blocks.answer: Dry mouth and skin, urinary retention, constipation, dilated pupils and tachycardia.

blocks.markdown: **Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors in myasthenia gravis.** Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease in which antibodies reduce the number of functional nicotinic ACh receptors at the neuromuscular junction. Each nerve impulse therefore produces a smaller end-plate potential, which fails more often during repeated use, so weakness worsens with exertion. AChE inhibitors such as **pyridostigmine** (long term) and **neostigmine** (shorter acting) prevent breakdown of ACh, so it persists in the cleft, binds the remaining receptors repeatedly and increases the chance of reaching the threshold for muscle contraction. They treat symptoms, not the underlying autoimmune process.

blocks.title: How an AChE inhibitor restores strength
blocks.prompt: Explain step by step why pyridostigmine improves muscle strength in myasthenia gravis, and why it can cause diarrhoea and salivation.

steps.text: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies reduce usable nicotinic receptors, so the same quantity of ACh released produces a smaller depolarisation of the muscle end-plate.
Pyridostigmine inhibits AChE, so ACh is not hydrolysed quickly; its concentration and duration of action in the cleft increase.
More receptors reach activation threshold and the end-plate potential is more likely to trigger a muscle action potential; strength improves.

The same inhibition acts at all cholinergic synapses, including muscarinic ones, so parasympathetic effects are enhanced: salivation, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, bradycardia and bronchial secretions. An antimuscarinic such as propantheline or hyoscine can be added to control them.

blocks.answer: AChE inhibition raises synaptic ACh and improves neuromuscular transmission; muscarinic overactivity explains the side effects.

blocks.title: Too much or too little
blocks.text: Excess ACh (AChE inhibitors, organophosphates) causes muscarinic overactivity (salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhoea, bradycardia, bronchoconstriction, miosis) plus nicotinic effects (fasciculations, weakness). Atropine reverses the muscarinic effects but not the nicotinic weakness.

blocks.markdown: **Anticholinergic toxicity** occurs after overdose or accumulation of drugs with antimuscarinic action, including atropine, hyoscine, tricyclic antidepressants, first-generation antihistamines (such as chlorphenamine) and antipsychotics. It produces a recognisable pattern from blocked muscarinic receptors in both the periphery and the central nervous system.

items: Peripheral: dry mouth, dry hot flushed skin, fever, dilated pupils with blurred vision, tachycardia, urinary retention, reduced bowel sounds and constipation.
Central: agitation, confusion, delirium, hallucinations, and in severe cases seizures or coma.
Mnemonic: hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter.
Management is mainly supportive (cooling, benzodiazepines for agitation or seizures, monitoring of the ECG); physostigmine is used only in selected cases under specialist guidance.

blocks.title: Older adults
blocks.text: Older people are particularly sensitive to drugs with antimuscarinic effects, which can cause acute confusion, urinary retention and constipation. Review drugs with anticholinergic burden before attributing new confusion to dementia.

blocks.title: Dry versus damp
blocks.text: Anticholinergic toxicity gives dry skin; sympathomimetic toxicity (for example cocaine or amphetamine) gives sweaty skin. Both produce dilated pupils and tachycardia, so skin moisture and bowel sounds are the quickest clue.

points: Muscarinic antagonists such as atropine block parasympathetic effects: tachycardia, mydriasis, dry secretions, urinary retention and constipation.
AChE inhibitors such as pyridostigmine raise synaptic ACh and restore neuromuscular transmission in myasthenia gravis, where nicotinic receptors are reduced by antibodies.
Anticholinergic toxicity presents with hot, dry, flushed skin, dilated pupils, tachycardia, retention and delirium, and is managed mainly supportively.

questions.stem: Which effect is expected after a therapeutic dose of atropine?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: blocking M2 receptors removes vagal slowing of the SA node.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: atropine causes mydriasis, not miosis.

questions.explanation: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors, removing parasympathetic tone. At the heart this removes vagal braking and the rate rises, and in other organs it causes drying and relaxation of smooth muscle.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man develops urinary retention and constipation after starting an antimuscarinic bladder drug for urgency. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Blockade of muscarinic receptors reduces detrusor contraction and gut motility
Stimulation of nicotinic receptors contracts the bladder sphincter
Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase raises parasympathetic tone
Blockade of beta-2 receptors relaxes the bowel

questions.correctOptionText: Blockade of muscarinic receptors reduces detrusor contraction and gut motility

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the parasympathetic drive to detrusor and bowel is muscarinic.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: the drug is not a nicotinic agonist.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: AChE inhibitors would increase bladder contraction and bowel motility.

questions.explanation: Detrusor contraction and bowel peristalsis depend on muscarinic stimulation. Blocking them reduces urinary urgency (the desired effect) but also causes retention and constipation as extensions of the same action.

questions.stem: What is the principal mechanism by which pyridostigmine improves weakness in myasthenia gravis?

options.text: It inhibits acetylcholinesterase, increasing acetylcholine in the neuromuscular junction
It removes the autoantibodies against the receptor
It blocks nicotinic receptors on the muscle
It increases the number of nicotinic receptors permanently

questions.correctOptionText: It inhibits acetylcholinesterase, increasing acetylcholine in the neuromuscular junction

distractorRationale.a: Correct: more ACh persists in the cleft to stimulate the reduced receptor population.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: this is the role of immunosuppression or plasma exchange.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: it does not change receptor number.

questions.explanation: Pyridostigmine slows ACh breakdown so each released quantum acts for longer and on more receptors. It treats symptoms only; immunosuppression addresses the autoimmune cause.

questions.stem: A patient with myasthenia gravis taking pyridostigmine develops abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, excessive salivation and a pulse of 48 beats/min. What explains these features?

options.text: Excess acetylcholine acting at muscarinic receptors

questions.correctOptionText: Excess acetylcholine acting at muscarinic receptors

distractorRationale.a: Correct: AChE inhibition enhances ACh at parasympathetic synapses as well as the neuromuscular junction.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: blockade would cause dry mouth and tachycardia.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: alpha-1 stimulation would cause vasoconstriction.

questions.explanation: AChE inhibition is not selective for the neuromuscular junction, so muscarinic effects (salivation, cramps, diarrhoea, bradycardia) appear when the dose is too high. This is a cholinergic excess and the dose should be reviewed.

questions.stem: Explain the pathophysiology of myasthenia gravis and how acetylcholinesterase inhibitors improve symptoms.
markingGuide: Autoantibodies against nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction reduce functional receptors
Smaller end-plate potential, so transmission fails with repeated use and weakness is fatigable
AChE inhibitors (pyridostigmine, neostigmine) block hydrolysis of ACh
Higher and longer-lasting synaptic ACh increases activation of remaining receptors and improves strength
Symptomatic only; does not treat the autoimmune cause; muscarinic side effects (diarrhoea, salivation, bradycardia) can occur
questions.explanation: Fewer receptors mean each nerve impulse produces a weaker response. AChE inhibition boosts ACh at the junction, partly compensating for the receptor loss.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old student arrives in the emergency department agitated, with hot dry skin, dilated pupils and a heart rate of 128 beats/min after ingesting an unknown quantity of tablets. Which toxidrome does this best fit?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: dry skin, mydriasis, tachycardia and agitation are typical.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: cholinergic toxicity gives salivation, sweating, miosis and bradycardia.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: opioids cause pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression.

questions.explanation: Hot, dry skin with dilated pupils and tachycardia reflects widespread muscarinic blockade, and agitation reflects the central effect. Cholinergic and opioid toxicity produce constricted pupils.

questions.stem: List the features of anticholinergic toxicity and explain how the skin findings help to distinguish it from sympathomimetic toxicity.
markingGuide: Peripheral: dry mouth, dry flushed skin, hyperthermia, mydriasis and blurred vision, tachycardia, urinary retention, reduced bowel sounds
Central: agitation, confusion, delirium, hallucinations, seizures or coma in severe cases
Sweating is lost because sweat glands are cholinergic (muscarinic) so skin is dry
Sympathomimetic toxicity also causes tachycardia and mydriasis but sweat glands are stimulated so skin is sweaty and bowel sounds are normal or increased
Management mainly supportive; benzodiazepines for agitation or seizures; physostigmine only in selected cases
questions.explanation: Sweat glands are sympathetic but cholinergic, so antimuscarinics stop sweating whereas adrenergic overload promotes it. The skin therefore separates two otherwise similar presentations.

questions.stem: A farmer is brought in after a spill of an organophosphate insecticide, with salivation, small pupils, sweating, bradycardia, wheeze and muscle fasciculations. Which treatment targets the muscarinic effects?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and reverses bradycardia, secretions and bronchoconstriction.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: neostigmine is an AChE inhibitor and would worsen the poisoning.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: pyridostigmine is also an AChE inhibitor.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: propranolol would worsen bradycardia and bronchospasm.

questions.explanation: Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit AChE, so ACh accumulates. Atropine antagonises the muscarinic consequences, although it does not reverse the nicotinic muscle weakness, which needs supportive care and specific antidotes such as pralidoxime under specialist guidance.

questions.stem: True or false: atropine can reverse the muscle weakness (fasciculations and paralysis) caused by excess acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction.
questions.explanation: Neuromuscular transmission uses nicotinic receptors, and atropine blocks only muscarinic receptors. It therefore treats the muscarinic features of cholinergic excess but not nicotinic muscle weakness.

questions.stem: Describe the actions of atropine on the heart, eye, glands, bladder and gut, and give two clinical uses.
markingGuide: Competitive muscarinic antagonist removing parasympathetic tone
Heart: tachycardia by blocking vagal action at SA and AV nodes
Salivary, bronchial and sweat glands: reduced secretion, dry mouth and dry skin
Bladder and gut: reduced detrusor contraction (retention) and reduced motility (constipation)
Uses: symptomatic bradycardia, organophosphate poisoning, reducing secretions before anaesthesia, mydriasis for eye examination
questions.explanation: Atropine's effects can all be predicted by removing parasympathetic tone from each organ. Its clinical uses exploit those effects, for example reversing vagal bradycardia.
